overview.headline: Classification, hazards, and storage of radioactive waste

keyPoints.point: There are two broad classifications of radioactive waste, high-level and low-level, determined by source and hazard.
keyPoints.quote: There are two broad classifications: high-level or low-level waste.

keyPoints.point: Fission products account for most heat and penetrating radiation in high-level waste.
keyPoints.quote: These isotopes, called "fission products," account for most of the heat and penetrating radiation in high-level waste.

keyPoints.point: Strontium-90 and cesium-137 have half-lives of about 30 years before half the radioactivity decays.
keyPoints.quote: Strontium-90 and cesium-137 have half-lives of about 30 years (half the radioactivity will decay in 30 years).

keyPoints.point: Water about 40 feet deep serves to shield radiation and cool rods in pools.
keyPoints.quote: The water is typically about 40 feet deep and serves both to shield the radiation and cool the rods.

keyPoints.point: The Department of Transportation regulates packaging and carriage of radioactive waste for transport.
keyPoints.quote: The Department of Transportation regulates both the packaging and carriage of all hazardous materials, including radioactive waste.

keyTerms.gloss: Isotopes that account for most heat and penetrating radiation in waste.
keyTerms.quote: These isotopes, called "fission products," account for most of the heat and penetrating radiation in high-level waste.

keyTerms.gloss: Elements heavier than uranium that take much longer to decay and remain hazardous.
keyTerms.quote: These heavier-than-uranium, or "transuranic," elements do not produce nearly the amount of heat or penetrating radiation that fission products do

keyTerms.gloss: Time for half the radioactivity to decay, about 30 years for some isotopes.
keyTerms.quote: Strontium-90 and cesium-137 have half-lives of about 30 years (half the radioactivity will decay in 30 years).

keyTerms.gloss: Pools that store spent fuel where water shields radiation and cools rods.
keyTerms.quote: All U.S. nuclear power plants store spent nuclear fuel in "spent fuel pools."

keyTerms.gloss: Stainless canisters surrounded by concrete used for storage after pool cooling.
keyTerms.quote: As the pools near capacity, utilities move some of the older spent fuel into “dry cask” storage.

keyTerms.gloss: Radioactive wastes disposed in near-surface facilities with no intent to recover.
keyTerms.quote: Low-level wastes, generally defined as radioactive wastes other than high-level and wastes from uranium recovery operations
